lesson.title: Adding Up Storage: Capacitors in Parallel
lesson.summary: Parallel capacitors all share the same voltage, so their capacitances simply add, effectively combining plate area into one larger charge reservoir.
lesson.body:
A parallel circuit connects components across the same two nodes, guaranteeing that every branch sees the identical voltage, a principle you already know from parallel circuits built with resistors. For capacitors, that shared voltage has a simple and useful consequence: since both plates of every parallel capacitor are tied to the same two shared nodes, connecting capacitors in parallel is electrically the same as increasing the amount of plate area facing the same gap and dielectric. More plate area at the same voltage means more charge can be stored, so capacitance in parallel simply adds.

The math confirms the intuition directly. Every capacitor in a parallel bank sees the same voltage V, so each one stores its own charge according to Q-i equals C-i times V. The total charge delivered by the source is the sum of all those individual charges, Q-total equals Q1 plus Q2 plus further terms, which expands to V times C1, plus V times C2, and so on, or V times the sum of all the capacitances. Since Q-total also equals C-total times V by definition, dividing both sides by V leaves C-total equals C1 plus C2 plus further terms, a plain sum with no reciprocals involved, the mirror image of how capacitors behave in series and the same pattern resistors follow when they are wired in series rather than parallel.

Take the same two capacitors used in the series example, but wire them in parallel instead: C1 at 4 microfarads and C2 at 12 microfarads. The combined capacitance is simply C1 plus C2, or 4 plus 12, equal to 16 microfarads, more than five times what the same pair produced in series. Connect that parallel pair to a 10 volt source and check the charge on each: Q1 equals C1 times V, or 4 microfarads times 10 volts, equal to 40 microcoulombs, and Q2 equals C2 times V, or 12 microfarads times 10 volts, equal to 120 microcoulombs. Adding those gives a total of 160 microcoulombs, and checking against the combined value directly, C-total times V equals 16 microfarads times 10 volts, which is also 160 microcoulombs, confirming the two methods agree.

This lines up perfectly with the physical capacitance formula from earlier, C equals epsilon times A divided by d. Putting capacitors in series is geometrically like stretching out the separation distance d between one effective set of plates, which is why series capacitance shrinks and behaves like adding resistances that oppose charge buildup. Putting capacitors in parallel is geometrically like welding more plate area A onto the same gap, which is why parallel capacitance simply grows with each addition.

Because parallel capacitance adds so cleanly, it is the standard trick for building up a specific bulk capacitance from parts that are readily available, and for spreading current demand across several smaller components rather than stressing one large one. It also shows up constantly in decoupling: a circuit board often places a bulk electrolytic capacitor of tens or hundreds of microfarads right next to several small ceramic capacitors in the nanofarad or picofarad range, all in parallel across the same power rail, since each capacitor type responds best over a different range of frequencies, and paralleling them lets the combination smooth out both slow and fast fluctuations in supply voltage at once.
